title: The Mughals: Akbar's Empire and the World's Silver

cards.h: An empire that held a quarter of the world's wealth
cards.b:
The Mughal Empire ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from the 1520s to the 1700s. One well-known estimate puts India at about a quarter of world output around 1700. That made it one of the richest places on Earth.

The Mughals were not just a regional power. They traded with Europe, Central Asia and Iran, and their silver, cloth and gunpowder helped shape a global economy.

Babur, a prince from Central Asia who claimed descent from Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India in 1526. At the first battle of Panipat he beat the Delhi sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, with cannon and matchlock guns. The name "Mughal" comes from the word Mongol.

Babur set up a dynasty that lasted for over three centuries. His memoir, the Baburnama, is one of the liveliest books written by any ruler of his age.

cards.h: Akbar and the peace with all
cards.b:
Akbar became emperor in 1556 at the age of thirteen. He built a strong army and a fair system of taxes, and he ruled from new cities such as Fatehpur Sikri. He made peace with many Rajput families by marriage and service.

Akbar's ideal was called sulh-i kul, or peace with all. He held discussions with Hindu, Muslim, Jain, Christian and Zoroastrian scholars, and he scrapped the pilgrim tax and later the jizya tax on non-Muslims.

Abul Fazl (1551–1602)

A close adviser to Akbar, Abul Fazl wrote the Ain-i-Akbari (The Institutes of Akbar) in the 1590s. It is a huge survey of the empire: its provinces, revenues, castes, crafts and army.

It is one of the most detailed sources for early modern India. It also presents Akbar in the best light, so it is an official voice.

cards.h: The Mughal story in key dates
cards.b: The Mughal peak came in the 1600s. The empire then faced rebellions, wars and invasions, and it slowly broke into regional states.

cards.h: The Peacock Throne and the Taj
cards.b:
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Work began in the 1630s, and the white marble tomb was largely completed by about 1653. He also commissioned the jewelled Peacock Throne, a symbol of Mughal wealth.

The Taj is famous today, but its building cost huge sums. Historians argue whether such projects were a sign of strength or a drain on the state.

cards.h: Was Mughal India a backward ruin?
cards.b:
A common view of the 1700s says that Mughal India was a decaying society until British rule rescued it. This picture was used to justify colonial conquest.

Historians argue that the Mughal economy was strong, with busy towns and large exports of cloth. Decline in some regions was real, but it was not the whole story. The Mughal state did weaken in the 1700s, and the causes are still debated.

The historian Marshall Hodgson called the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals the "gunpowder empires". Their rulers used cannon and muskets, and they paid large armies with taxes raised from fertile farmland.

Historians argue that guns alone did not make empires. Administration, tax systems, alliances and trade were just as important.

The Mughal rupee was a silver coin of good quality, and it helped create a single currency across much of the empire. Silver from the Americas and Japan reached India through European traders, and it was spent on Indian goods.

Indian cotton cloth was sold across Asia, to Africa and to Europe. The Dutch and English East India Companies set up trading posts at Surat, Hooghly and other ports to buy it.

Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707. He pushed the empire deep into the Deccan and fought long wars against the Marathas and the Deccan sultanates. His armies were huge, and his campaigns were costly.

When he died in 1707, the empire was stretched thin. Regional governors and Maratha leaders gained power. Historians argue whether the decline came from overreach, from local resistance or from a changing economy.

Mughal painting blended Persian, Indian and European styles. Persian poetry and language were the court's tongue, and Urdu and Hindustani flourished in the cities. The gardens, forts and mosques of the Mughals still shape Indian cities today.

Indian and world historians now see the Mughals not as a foreign rule alone, but as a mixed and creative culture. That view changes how we read every Indian dynasty since.

In 1600, while Akbar ruled, English merchants in London founded the East India Company. In 1615 the envoy Thomas Roe reached the court of Jahangir, Akbar's son, to win trading rights in the empire.

The Mughals welcomed trade but did not expect Europeans to challenge their power. That was a costly mistake for the empire's future, and it shaped the path that led to British rule in India.

Five things to remember
  1. Babur won the first battle of Panipat in 1526.
  2. Akbar ruled from 1556 and promoted sulh-i kul.
  3. Abul Fazl wrote the Ain-i-Akbari.
  4. The Taj Mahal was largely complete by about 1653.
  5. Aurangzeb died in 1707, and the empire weakened after him.
Think about it
  • Did the Mughals build a strong state, or one that depended on a few strong rulers?
  • Why did a rich empire end up in decline?
